Place compass near North pole; mark pencil dots at needle tip (N) and tail (S).
Move compass so tail sits exactly on the previous tip dot; mark new tip dot.
Repeat stepping across paper until compass reaches South pole; join dots with smooth curve.
Repeat from various starting points around magnet to map full vector field.
observation: Continuous smooth field lines emerge from the North pole, curve through surrounding space, and enter the South pole without intersecting at any point.
concept: A magnetic field line is the trajectory along which a theoretical isolated North magnetic pole would move. Two magnetic field lines can never cross; if they did, a compass placed at the intersection would point in two contradictory directions simultaneously.
equation: Tangent to field line at point P = Direction of B vector  ;  ∇ · B = 0 (No magnetic monopoles)

quiz.question: Why can two magnetic field lines never cross or intersect each other?
answers: At the point of intersection, the compass needle would have to point in two different directions simultaneously, which is physically impossible
Magnetic field drops to zero between lines
quiz.explanation: The tangent to a field line gives the unique direction of the magnetic field vector. If two lines intersected, the field would have two different directions at that single point, which is physically impossible.

safety: Store plotting compasses away from strong magnetic fields to prevent demagnetization or polarity reversal.

title: Magnetic Field of a Circular Current Loop
subject: Physics
apparatus: Thick circular copper loop / multi-turn coil mounted through horizontal cardboard, 6V DC battery, iron filings, compasses, rheostat, switch.
steps: Pass circular copper wire loop vertically through two holes in a horizontal cardboard sheet.
Sprinkle iron filings uniformly over cardboard and close switch to pass 5A DC current.
Gently tap cardboard to reveal magnetic field pattern.
Use plotting compasses to trace field lines near wire conductors and across the loop center.
observation: Near the wire segments, field lines form concentric circles. As you move towards the loop center, the curved circular arcs flatten out into straight, parallel lines perpendicular to the loop plane.
concept: Every infinitesimal current segment contributes vectorially to the total field (Biot-Savart Law). At the coil center, magnetic contributions from all loop segments add constructively in the same direction, generating a strong uniform magnetic field.
equation: B_center = (μ₀ · N · I) / (2 · R)  ;  Clock Face Rule: Clockwise current = South Pole ; Anticlockwise = North Pole

quiz.question: If you look at one circular face of a current-carrying coil and the current flows in a clockwise direction, what magnetic pole does that face represent?
quiz.explanation: By the Clock Face Rule, if current flows in a clockwise direction around the perimeter, that face acts as a South magnetic pole; anticlockwise current represents a North pole.

safety: High currents in circular coils generate resistive heat. Use an intermittent tap key to prevent overheating.

title: Force on a Wire Carrying Current in a Magnetic Field
subject: Physics
apparatus: Light aluminium rod (AB) suspended horizontally by flexible copper leads, strong permanent horseshoe magnet, 6V battery, reversing switch, retort stand.
steps: Suspend aluminium rod AB horizontally between the vertical poles of horseshoe magnet (magnetic field B directed upwards from N to S).
Pass current through rod from end B to end A; observe direction of mechanical displacement.
Reverse current direction (from A to B) and observe reversed rod displacement.
Interchange magnet poles (field directed downwards) and verify Fleming's Left-Hand Rule.
observation: When current flows through the rod in the magnetic field, the rod experiences an immediate sideways mechanical thrust and swings outward. Reversing either current or magnetic field reverses displacement direction.
concept: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a Lorentz magnetic force: F = I(L × B). The direction of force is perpendicular to both current and magnetic field, predicted by Fleming's Left-Hand Rule.
equation: F = B · I · L · sin(θ)  ;  Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: Forefinger = Field (B), Center finger = Current (I), Thumb = Force (F)

quiz.question: According to Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, which finger represents the direction of the mechanical force (motion) acting on the conductor?
quiz.explanation: In Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: Forefinger represents magnetic Field, Center finger represents Current, and Thumb points in the direction of mechanical Force (Motion).

safety: Ensure flexible leads allow free swinging motion without short-circuiting against the steel magnet body.

title: Electromagnetic Induction by Moving a Magnet
subject: Physics
apparatus: Multi-turn insulated copper wire solenoid coil (N = 500 turns), strong permanent bar magnet, sensitive center-zero galvanometer (G), connecting leads.
steps: Connect solenoid terminals directly to a sensitive center-zero galvanometer (no battery in circuit).
Plunge North pole of bar magnet rapidly into the coil interior; observe galvanometer needle kick.
Hold magnet completely stationary inside the coil; observe galvanometer needle position.
Withdraw magnet rapidly from coil; observe needle kick in the opposite direction.
Test effect of moving magnet slowly vs rapidly, and repeat with South pole.
observation: Moving the magnet into the coil causes instantaneous needle deflection to the right. When the magnet stops moving, deflection returns to ZERO. Withdrawing magnet deflects needle to the left. Faster motion produces greater deflection.
concept: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction: an induced electromotive force (EMF) and current are generated in a closed circuit whenever the magnetic flux linking the circuit changes with time. Stationary flux produces zero induced current.
equation: Induced EMF ε = −N · (dΦ_B / dt)  ;  Φ_B = ∫ B · dA  ;  Lenz's Law: Induced current opposes the flux change

quiz.question: What happens to the galvanometer reading when a strong bar magnet is held completely stationary inside a conducting solenoid?
answers: The galvanometer needle rests precisely at zero (no induced current)
The needle shows constant maximum deflection
quiz.explanation: Electromagnetic induction requires a changing magnetic flux (dΦ/dt ≠ 0). When the magnet is stationary relative to the coil, flux is constant (dΦ/dt = 0), so induced EMF is strictly zero.

safety: Center-zero galvanometers are highly sensitive instruments; avoid dropping or subjecting to heavy mechanical shocks.

title: Induction Between Neighbouring Coils (Mutual Induction)
subject: Physics
apparatus: Primary coil P (with battery and tapping key), Secondary coil S (connected to sensitive galvanometer), soft iron cylindrical core, connecting wires.
steps: Wind Primary coil P and Secondary coil S side-by-side over a common non-conducting cylinder or soft iron core.
Connect Primary coil to battery and tapping key; connect Secondary coil to galvanometer.
Press tapping key to close primary circuit; observe momentary galvanometer kick in secondary.
Hold key continuously closed (steady primary current); observe galvanometer reading.
Release tapping key to open primary circuit; observe momentary galvanometer kick in opposite direction.
observation: A momentary transient deflection appears in the secondary coil only at the exact instant primary current is switched ON or switched OFF. While primary current is steady DC, secondary galvanometer reads exactly ZERO.
concept: Mutual induction is the phenomenon whereby a time-varying current in a primary coil creates a time-varying magnetic flux that links a neighbouring secondary coil, inducing an electromotive force: ε₂ = −M (dI₁/dt).
equation: ε₂ = −M · (dI₁ / dt)  ;  M = Mutual Inductance (Henries)  ;  Steady DC (dI/dt = 0) → ε₂ = 0

quiz.question: When a steady, unchanging direct current (DC) flows through the primary coil, what is the induced current in the neighbouring secondary coil?
quiz.explanation: A steady direct current creates a constant, unchanging magnetic flux. Because mutual induction requires a rate of change of flux (dΦ/dt), a steady DC primary induces zero EMF in the secondary.

safety: Sudden opening of inductive primary circuits can produce a high back-EMF spark across switch contacts.
